S01: Packet analysis can explain a slow lesson download, an unexpected address change, or a suspicious name response.
Throughout this lesson, we will name the observation point before interpreting the traffic.
All Northstar evidence in this package is synthetic teaching material.
S02: Sniffing means observing network traffic through a capture interface or another collection point.
An IP address identifies a network endpoint in the packet.
A conversation view is an interpretation assembled from that sample.
At Northstar, a connection to a classroom service may support troubleshooting.
S03: The teacher laptop, STAFF, keeps its address at ten dot forty-four dot ten dot twenty-one.
The shared campus map is unchanged.
A packet going to the DNS server in another subnet normally has the DNS server's destination IP but the local gateway's destination MAC on the office segment.
This distinction will help us interpret ARP and identify capture placement.
S04: A useful capture plan begins with a question, such as whether STAFF received competing DNS answers during a known time window.
Even a short capture can contain names, cookies, messages, or other sensitive information.
We will not open a live interface, redirect a neighbor's traffic, or start a DHCP service.
Preparing this lesson does not establish that a learner performed such a lab.
S05: Ethernet uses source and destination MAC addresses to deliver frames on a local link.
An ordinary unicast destination identifies one link-layer recipient.
Read the capture's link type before applying Ethernet assumptions: a file containing another link-layer format may expose different fields.
Then ask how the receiving switch would forward that frame.
S06: A learning Ethernet switch associates source MAC addresses with the ports on which it observes them, within the relevant VLAN.
Broadcast traffic and some unknown unicast traffic can be flooded within the applicable forwarding domain.
To evaluate a missing packet, ask whether the switch had any reason to deliver it to the observation port.
S07: An interface normally filters some received traffic before passing it to the operating system.
A capture on ANALYST can still miss STAFF's known unicast traffic.
When someone claims to have captured an entire network by selecting promiscuous mode, ask for the collection topology and switch configuration.
At Northstar, document whether the source was an endpoint interface, a configured mirror destination, or a network tap.
S08: A VLAN defines a logical Layer Two broadcast domain.
The destination IP continues to identify the server while link-layer addresses change across routed links.
In the drawing, trace one packet through the office link and then show the newly framed server-side hop.
The gateway and the DNS server play different roles.
S09: Suppose a teacher says a page loaded slowly.
None of these sources alone covers every possible cause.
Two dashboards based on the same capture are also not two independent observations.
This lets a reviewer distinguish a measured packet count from an inferred explanation.
S10: An endpoint capture is often the easiest place to begin a focused investigation.
A packet shown with an apparent bad checksum may have been captured before hardware completed the checksum.
An endpoint trace can miss traffic on another interface, outside the capture interval, or discarded before the collection hook.
Compare suspicious results with a suitable independent observation when necessary.
S11: A switch port analyzer session, often called SPAN or port mirroring, copies selected traffic to a monitoring destination.
A mirror can also drop copies when selected traffic exceeds destination capacity or device resources.
A capture file alone rarely proves those settings.
Their differences are teaching assumptions encoded in the fixture manifest.
S12: A network tap provides a dedicated way to observe traffic on a link.
The collector still needs sufficient capacity and an appropriate link-layer decoder.
For analysis, preserve documentation of the monitored link and how the capture was produced.
Compare endpoint, mirror, and tap approaches by the specific question and coverage needed.
S13: Our first executable workflow reads a supplied capture file offline.
The bundled verification then invokes tcpdump with a file input, numeric address output, and a stated filter.
The network events represented by those bytes remain fictional.
If an expected result differs, retain the original file and command before changing anything.
S14: A capture filter selects which packets are admitted by the capture mechanism.
Wireshark expressions such as an IP address comparison belong to that second language.
At Northstar, save the exact expression and whether it was applied during collection or analysis.
The Wireshark worksheet supplies separate display expressions.
S15: Select a conversation by addresses and transport ports, then inspect its packet sequence.
A partial capture can begin after establishment or end before a response.
Stream reconstruction can help read application data, but missing segments and analyzer assumptions still matter.
If a synthetic HTTP response contains an ordinary teaching message, that is the content supplied by the fixture.
S16: A capture's absence of an expected packet supports a limited conclusion: it was not present in the retained data under the recorded collection conditions.
A header may survive while application content is cut off.
Record relevant counters and settings when a real lab supplies them.
The synthetic fixtures have declared complete record lengths for their constructed packets.
S17: Plaintext application traffic can expose request paths, headers, and message bodies to a collector on the communication path.
It does not establish that a third party's traffic was redirected or that an application accepted a login.
At Northstar, use the example to explain why sensitive services need protected transport and careful logging.
A capture containing secrets can become a sensitive artifact itself.
S18: TLS provides a protected channel when negotiated and authenticated correctly.
Some metadata can remain visible, including IP endpoints, transport information, packet sizes, and timing.
At Northstar, compare the readable HTTP teaching message with a clearly labeled conceptual TLS record diagram.
Encryption limits payload inspection, while endpoint and service logs may provide other authorized evidence.
S19: A virtual private network can protect traffic across an untrusted path by carrying it inside a protected tunnel.
An observer outside the tunnel may see outer addresses and timing while losing access to inner content.
At Northstar, draw the classroom application path and mark exactly where the tunnel begins and ends.
This avoids treating a tunnel icon as a universal privacy guarantee.
S20: Some traditional application protocols were designed without modern transport protection.
A port number alone cannot establish which protection is active.
A defense plan can replace an exposed management path with an authenticated encrypted alternative, restrict who can reach it, and verify that old access paths are actually closed.
Keep availability requirements and device capabilities explicit.
S21: We can now separate three questions.
A capture may answer the first two partly while leaving the third open.
At Northstar, use a service configuration check, an authorized endpoint observation, and a bounded capture together when appropriate.
In an incident brief, say exactly which payload was readable and which remained unexamined.
S22: Address Resolution Protocol, or ARP, helps a host discover the Ethernet address associated with an IPv4 address on its local link.
When STAFF communicates with an off-subnet destination, the relevant local mapping is normally the gateway's IPv4 address.
That design creates opportunities for false mappings when additional protections are absent.
Our fixture shows explicit teaching mappings and replies.
S23: ARP poisoning attempts to persuade a recipient to associate a local IPv4 address with an inappropriate MAC address.
A false reply alone does not prove successful bidirectional interception, content reading, or data theft.
This supports the observation that the supplied trace contains conflicting binding claims.
It does not include a real cache change or actual forwarding path.
S24: A changed gateway mapping deserves investigation, but it can have legitimate explanations.
At Northstar, compare the old and new MAC addresses with the approved gateway inventory, maintenance window, and switch observations.
Our fictional approval card deliberately leaves the change unconfirmed so the student must state a next check.
This approach supports a timely protective decision while preserving uncertainty about cause.
S25: Dynamic ARP Inspection, or DAI, can validate ARP traffic against trusted binding information and configured policy on supporting switches.
Trusted ports are an important configuration boundary; trusting the wrong path can bypass intended inspection, while rejecting legitimate traffic can disrupt service.
Verify the expected forwarding or rejection and the relevant logs.
Product support and exact commands vary by platform and release.
S26: Sniffing courses name tools that can observe ARP, generate address claims, or combine redirection with analysis.
Knowing a tool name is useful for recognizing its role, but running a command successfully does not establish that a recipient changed its cache or that traffic was intercepted.
At Northstar, a complete success criterion for any later lab would identify recipient state, traffic direction, control behavior, and retained evidence.
That criterion should exist before choosing an active tool.
S27: MAC spoofing changes the link-layer address an interface presents.
A simple MAC allowlist can constrain a narrow environment, but it is not equivalent to strong user or device authentication.
Do not infer a unique physical machine solely from a vendor prefix.
A defensive explanation should state what the control binds, how changes are authorized, and which observation verifies the expected state.
S28: A MAC flooding technique attempts to stress a switch's address-learning resources by presenting many source addresses.
Do not teach that every modern switch becomes a hub when its table is full.
There is no flooding generator in this package.
A packet count alone cannot establish table exhaustion.
S29: Port security can limit or constrain learned source addresses on supported access ports.
A virtualization host can present several.
Review counters, logs, and recovery behavior, then validate both accepted and rejected traffic in the permitted lab.
A successful configuration command proves that the device accepted a setting, not that the entire defense works.
S30: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol helps a client obtain network configuration.
Correlate the transaction identifier, client information, message type, and relevant options.
Our synthetic file includes a discovery and competing offers.
Consequently, it cannot show which offer the client accepted or which configuration became active.
S31: DHCP starvation attempts to consume available leases or related resources so legitimate clients cannot obtain expected configuration.
A burst of discoveries alone does not establish that a pool was exhausted.
At Northstar, E03 presents two offers for one constructed transaction, including different router options.
A next check would identify the sending ports, authorized servers, and the client's selected configuration.
S32: DHCP snooping can distinguish trusted server-facing paths from untrusted client-facing paths and build binding information on supported switches.
Those dependencies mean that an incomplete or incorrect binding state can affect several controls.
Validate that a legitimate client obtains the correct lease and that an unauthorized teaching offer is handled as intended in an isolated lab.
Preserve the binding table, relevant counters, and client configuration.
S33: VLAN hopping describes techniques that attempt to cross an intended Layer Two separation.
These are not universal properties of every switched network, and the exact prerequisites matter.
At Northstar, use the diagram to audit access-port roles, explicit trunk configuration, allowed VLANs, and native-VLAN choices against the intended design.
A defensive validation should test approved connectivity and isolation between named roles using the actual platform configuration.
S34: A VLAN defense begins with an accurate port inventory.
Review allowed VLANs, native-VLAN behavior, and the handling of unused ports according to the platform and design.
Both are useful, and neither proves every possible route.
Preserve the source and destination roles, timing, expected result, and actual result.
S35: Spanning Tree Protocol helps prevent loops in an Ethernet topology with redundant links.
This can change traffic paths or availability.
Then compare a reported topology change with maintenance records and actual device state.
Any later lab must identify the protocol variant, platform, configuration, and measured change.
S36: BPDU Guard and Root Guard address different expectations in a spanning-tree design.
These features are not interchangeable names for blocking every topology change.
Plan the availability effect, alerting, and recovery process, because enforcement may block or disable a path.
A protection that prevents a test event but breaks the approved teaching network needs correction.
S37: DNS connects a queried name and type to returned data under a hierarchy of zones, resolvers, and caches.
Generating a false local response and poisoning a recursive cache are distinct outcomes; both require acceptance evidence.
At Northstar, the synthetic file supplies two responses for the same constructed question and transaction, with different returned addresses.
Compare the approved zone data and resolver logs to determine what should have been returned under those conditions.
S38: DNSSEC can provide origin authentication and integrity for signed DNS data when the validation chain and policy support it.
Resolver trust, endpoint configuration, validation behavior, and the authoritative zone still matter.
These can complement one another without being equivalent.
A later verification should record the chosen resolver, relevant policy, response validation state, expected record, and actual client behavior.
S39: Passive sniffing observes traffic available at a collection point without deliberately changing another station's path.
These categories describe mechanisms, not whether an activity is authorized.
The animation can show how a path might change without causing that change on a real network.
A packet analyzer screenshot may be passive observation of an already supplied file, not proof that the operator performed the active technique illustrated beside it.
S40: Detecting a sniffer is challenging because a collector may transmit very little or nothing while it observes.
Nmap names one such local-Ethernet test sniffer-detect and classifies it as intrusive.
The state needs an approved purpose and owner before it becomes an incident conclusion.
A defensible detection statement names the mechanism tested, its expected signal, the collection conditions, and the uncovered cases.
S41: Wireshark provides interactive protocol inspection and display filtering.
Binding monitors can report changes in observed address relationships, while switch telemetry can describe ports and control behavior.
It does not invent a TShark execution receipt when that executable is unavailable.
If you run them later, save the actual version and result.
S42: A false positive occurs when a detection interprets benign activity as the harmful condition of interest.
An accurate alert that a MAC mapping changed can be followed by an incorrect inference that an attacker caused it.
At Northstar, compare the proposed ARP, DHCP, and DNS interpretations with maintenance records, client state, and collection coverage.
Broadly disabling a noisy sensor removes evidence as well as noise.
S43: An evidence ledger makes reasoning inspectable.
Use the word synthetic where the underlying traffic was generated for teaching.
A missing client acknowledgment may leave acceptance unknown.
When several records share one source, mark their dependency.
S44: Northstar's first case compares two synthetic observation points.
The fixture manifest names these assumptions, and the actual offline validator counts their bytes and packets.
The student should identify which file supports the question and whether any filter further narrowed the visible rows.
Choose the minimum suitable evidence rather than the largest possible file.
S45: E02 contains an initial reply associating the office gateway address with the approved teaching MAC, followed by another reply associating that same protocol address with a different MAC.
The supplied approval card has no confirmed gateway replacement for that interval.
Therefore, the brief should describe conflicting claims and request the appropriate independent records.
If such an action is merely proposed, keep it proposed.
S46: E03 shows a constructed DHCP discovery followed by two offers using the same transaction context.
The offline analysis identifies both offers and their declared fields.
We cannot claim that STAFF selected the unexpected gateway, that every client was affected, or that the authorized lease pool was exhausted.
Each check addresses a different remaining claim.
S47: E04 supplies a DNS query and two matching teaching responses that return different documentation addresses for the same classroom name.
The packet bytes support a conflict in the supplied response set.
At Northstar, request the approved resolver configuration, authoritative record state, and client behavior for the same interval.
A DNS-security recommendation should address the supported weakness and its prerequisites.
S48: The four Northstar cases share a teaching network and a method of reasoning.
Preserve the fixture identities and the fictional approval cards.
If new evidence later establishes client acceptance or a changed forwarding path, strengthen only the claims it actually supports.
S49: A layered defense addresses different parts of the communication path.
Monitoring can reveal unexpected changes and support investigation.
Enabling DAI does not establish correct TLS hostname validation.
Include rollback criteria when an operational change can interrupt teaching.
S50: After a defensive change, repeat the relevant observation under comparable conditions.
Then check the specific unwanted condition in the approved isolated environment.
Our source package supplies a checklist and synthetic analysis results, not a completed live-control test.
At Northstar, the owner signs off only on the scope actually exercised.
S51: A useful handoff lets another analyst reproduce the supported finding.
Our fixtures contain fictional teaching data, but their provenance still matters.
Do not label a proposed defense as deployed or a source-ready lesson as learner practice.
A reviewer should be able to trace every concrete claim back to a file, field, or qualified source.
S52: An AI assistant can help explain a protocol field, suggest a display filter, or organize a small evidence table.
Supply only approved, minimized data and keep real captures or secrets within their authorized custody.
At Northstar, an assistant might identify the two gateway claims, but a person must still check the addresses, approved change records, and scope of the conclusion.
Our teaching discussion does not claim that an AI system actually analyzed a live network or deployed a defense.
S53: Imagine an assistant reads the Northstar cards and writes that an attacker stole every teacher's password.
None proves accepted configuration, a complete interception path, actual credentials, or data transfer to an attacker.
This is a practical review pattern: identify the exact claim, inspect its cited source, state what that source directly supports, and name the evidence needed to go further.
Use AI to improve organization and question quality while preserving those boundaries.
S54: It does not cause an upstream switch to copy every other port.
The original capture filter becomes a display filter C.
A invents missing bytes, B treats different languages as interchangeable, and D claims coverage without the required collection evidence.
S55: Recipient cache changes, actual forwarding, impact, and approval each require additional evidence.
The color Wireshark assigns to UDP B.
Repeated dashboards may derive from the same underlying packet and add no independent observation.
S56: Neither feature guarantees every answer in every situation.
Treat all missing responses as successful attack suppression C.
S57: B preserves the useful observations and identifies how to reduce uncertainty.
Erase the failed service result from the report C.
C generalizes beyond the tested condition.
S58: Your capstone is a concise packet-analysis brief for the Northstar decision owner.
Compare the endpoint and mirror views, then inspect the ARP, DHCP, DNS, and harmless HTTP examples.
Record your own choice and confidence for each film question before consulting the separate answer key.
When learner execution is activated, save your actual brief, result or blocker, and rubric review in the CEH workspace.
